bib.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
authors: et al. (about 114 authors, Percy Liang last)

read.skipped: References (chars 571491 to 855562) skimmed for lineage only, not read line by line.

question: What are the capabilities, technical principles, applications and societal impacts of foundation models (models trained on broad data and adapted to many downstream tasks), and what opportunities and risks follow?
contributions: Introduces the term foundation model and the framing of emergence and homogenization
A 26-section interdisciplinary survey grouped into capabilities, applications, technology and society
Ecosystem view from data creation to deployment, with the rule 'think ecosystem, act model'
Proposes intrinsic vs extrinsic evaluation of foundation models and accounting for adaptation resources

results.claim: Homogenization means flaws in a foundation model are inherited by every adapted model downstream.
results.setup: Conceptual argument; no experiment.
results.quote: any flaws in the model are blindly inherited by all adapted models

results.claim: Almost all state-of-the-art NLP models are adapted from one of a few foundation models (BERT, RoBERTa, BART, T5).
results.setup: Scope is state-of-the-art NLP models as of 2021, not all AI systems.
results.quote:
Almost all state-of-
the-art NLP models are now adapted from one of a few foundation models, such as BERT, RoBERTa,
BART, T5, etc.

limits: Survey of 2021 state of the field: GPT-3 era, before instruction-tuned assistants, RLHF chat models and scaling to current systems; claims about models are dated.
The authors state that not all views are held by all authors and that the report is inevitably incomplete (Sec 1.4).
Almost no new experiments; most numbers are reported from cited work.
Does not use the terms hallucination or base-vs-assistant; factuality appears only as a concern in law and evaluation sections.
This extraction read only the sections listed in read.skipped.
Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3 are largely forward-looking visions with few measurements; the law section's GPT-3 transcript is a single worked example.
Sec 4.1 and 4.5-4.8 are position and design discussion: the numbers they carry are quoted from other work (Megatron, CLIP, Carlini and Terzis) rather than measured by the authors.
Sec 4.7 uses single point of failure in a security sense (poisoning, adversarial transfer, privacy); the hallucination link is the training-objective discussion in Sec 4.9.2.
Sec 4.8 itself says foundation models are not a panacea for distribution shift (spurious correlations, temporal drift).
Sec 4.10 excludes in-context learning from its pretrain/adapt modularization and says emergent behaviour may need the architecture opened up (Sec 4.10.3).
Sec 4.11 concedes that explanation methods may be unfaithful and that interpretability can be used to ethics-wash.
Sec 5.1-5.3 are position and framework sections: the numbers are quoted from other work (Strubell, Henderson, DiResta) and the break-even in Fig 27 is hypothetical.
Sec 5.3 concedes energy and carbon calculations are uncertain and that parameter count need not track energy efficiency.
Sec 5.1.4 concedes that technical bias mitigation is severely limited and that intrinsic-bias measures are brittle.
Sec 5.4 and 5.5 are US-law and economics commentary with no experiments; Sec 5.4 says it is centred on US law and the legal landscape is uncertain.
Sec 5.6.1 says more research is needed on how far training on similar data homogenizes failures in adapted derivatives.
Sec 5.6.3-5.6.5 are normative recommendations; the authors say they aim primarily to encourage dialogue about norms.
Sec 5.6.3 says tracing a harm to its source is unlikely to change the model without frameworks for attributing responsibility and recourse.
practices: Think ecosystem, act model: reason about a foundation model's social impact with surrogate downstream metrics and documentation (Sec 1.2).
Put warning labels on research models not fit to deploy and subject deployed models to rigorous testing and auditing (Sec 1.2).
Add application-specific logic (classifiers, output restrictions, validation of answers against documents) downstream to mitigate harms (Sec 1.2, adaptation stage).
Choose an adaptation method by compute budget, task data available and access to model gradients (Sec 4.3.1).
In evaluation, report adaptation resources and go beyond accuracy: robustness, fairness, efficiency, environmental impact (Sec 4.4.4).
Combine intrinsic evaluation with broad extrinsic evaluation of adapted models (Sec 4.4.5).
Use gradual releases for large deployments (Sec 1.2).
Developers should seek more predictable behaviour from foundation models via fine-tuning, prompt engineering, calibration or pre-formatting a task-specific endpoint (Sec 2.5.1).
If foundation models are pursued as a route to language understanding, multimodal training is likely the most viable strategy (Sec 2.6.4).
In healthcare, ensure training and evaluation data represent different sexes, races, ethnicities and socioeconomic backgrounds (Sec 3.1.3).
Separate explicit facts (external memory) from implicit knowledge (weights) to ease update, provenance and trust (Sec 4.1.4).
Record an adapted model's lineage (what it was adapted from) so errors can be traced to pretraining or adaptation (Sec 4.5.3).
Use behavioural testing and model assertions as unit-test analogues for production monitoring of foundation models (Sec 4.5.4).
Document datasets with datasheets or data statements and track licences, PII and consent in a data hub (Sec 4.6.2).
Consider freezing the foundation model and training a head or lightweight tuning for better OOD performance than full fine-tuning (Sec 4.8.3).
Test capabilities with bespoke controlled evaluations that need only input/output access (Sec 4.11.1).
Treat self-generated explanations sceptically because plausible text is not true insight (Sec 4.11.2).
Report computational, energy and carbon costs and any mitigation used (Sec 5.3.3).
Train in low-carbon-intensity regions and prefer efficient architectures, mixed precision, quantization and distillation before relying on offsets (Sec 5.3.1).
Document intrinsic biases and extrinsic harms, and use user studies of adapted models to document them (Sec 5.1.2).
Establish channels for harm feedback to reach upstream foundation model providers (Sec 5.1.4).
Foundation model developers bear greater responsibility of care than standard model developers because of widespread downstream effect (Sec 5.6.1).
Communicate clearly the realistic capabilities and limitations of foundation models to agencies adopting them (Sec 5.6.2).
Evaluate with ecological validity and ongoing evaluation rather than assuming benchmark gains translate to outcomes (Sec 5.6.2).
Stage releases with audits, ideally with a neutral staged release board choosing early-access recipients (Sec 5.6.4).
Host open API access for auditors, including gradient access and training-data access (Sec 5.6.4).
Create public issue-tracking-style reporting mechanisms so downstream users reach foundation model providers (Sec 5.6.3).
Label adapted derivatives with their foundation model and data in a model card or nutrition label (Sec 5.6.3).
Let individuals opt out of being data or decision subjects without repercussion (Sec 5.6.2, 5.6.6).

terms.definition: any model that is trained on broad data (generally using self-supervision at scale) that can be adapted (e.g., fine-tuned) to a wide range of downstream tasks
the behavior of a system is implicitly induced rather than explicitly constructed
the consolidation of methodologies for building machine learning systems across a wide range of applications; it provides strong leverage towards many tasks but also creates single points of failure
evaluation of the foundation model itself, divorced from a specific task
evaluation of task-specific models, dependent on both the foundation model and the adaptation mechanism
many adaptations of the same foundation model for automated decisions mean decision subjects face a more homogeneous set of judgments (Kleinberg and Raghavan 2021)
incoherent lapses suggest that models are merely 'stochastic parrots' (Bender et al. 2021), quoted in the philosophy section
a data management toolkit supporting interactive management of the foundation model data lifecycle (scale, integration, governance, quality)
a foundation model adapted to many applications through which attacks against it affect all adapted applications
the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance
the question whether a foundation model's behaviours share generalizable mechanisms (one model) or are independent task experts (many models)
the condition under which small population pretraining loss implies small minimal adaptation loss
properties of the foundation model that indirectly but pervasively affect downstream applications
harms arising in the context of specific downstream applications
people using foundation models as intended but with capabilities intentionally leveraged to cause harm
technologies like steam engine and electricity that drive transformation through pervasiveness, improvement over time and ability to spawn complementary innovations
decision subjects facing a more homogeneous set of judgments rooted in the same underlying foundation model, after Creel and Hellman 2021
a model produced by adapting a foundation model for a downstream task
a neutral body deciding which individuals or organizations get early access in a staged release
